quiz.q: By default, what happens if you try to reassign a variable created with `let`?
options: It works fine; variables are mutable by default
The compiler errors: cannot assign twice to an immutable variable
It silently creates a new variable
It only fails if the type changes
quiz.explain: Variables are immutable by default. Reassigning without `mut` gives 'cannot assign twice to immutable variable'.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `mut` and shadowing?
options: They are two names for the same thing
mut changes a value in place (same type); shadowing makes a new variable that can change type
mut only works on numbers, shadowing only on text
quiz.explain: `mut` reassigns the same variable and the type must stay the same. Shadowing (`let x` again) creates a brand-new variable, which may even have a different type.

quiz.q: What does `let x = 5; let x = x + 1;` do?
options: Creates a new variable x (shadowing) whose value is 6; the old one is hidden
Creates two variables both visible at once
quiz.explain: The second `let x` shadows the first — a new variable reusing the name. The old x is hidden, not mutated.

quiz.q: You wrote `let mut n = 3;` but never change `n`. What does Rust do?
options: Warns that the variable does not need to be mutable
quiz.explain: Rust warns 'variable does not need to be mutable' — a hint that your `mut` and your actual usage disagree.

flashcards.front: How do you make a variable changeable?
flashcards.back: Add `mut`: `let mut x = 5;`. Without it, variables are immutable by default.
Writing `let` again with the same name. It creates a NEW variable (the old one is hidden) and it may have a different type.

flashcards.front: mut vs shadowing — the one-line difference
flashcards.back: mut = same variable changes in place, type stays the same. Shadowing = new variable reusing the name, type can change.
A value fixed at compile time, always UPPER_SNAKE_CASE with an explicit type, e.g. `const MAX: u32 = 3;`. Never uses mut.
